blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A curve of three segments is written with fills f1, f2, f3 between 0 and 1, binaries w1 and w2, and the rows f2 <= w1 <= f1 and f3 <= w2 <= f2. Which fills does the model accept?

options.text: f1 = 0.5, f2 = 0.5, f3 = 0, as every fill is between 0 and 1
options.says: f2 = 0.5 needs w1 >= 0.5, so w1 = 1, and then w1 <= f1 asks for f1 = 1.

options.text: f1 = 1, f2 = 0.4, f3 = 0, as segment 1 is full before 2 starts
options.says: Right: w1 = 1 is allowed by f1 = 1, and w2 = 0 keeps f3 at 0, which it is.

options.text: f1 = 1, f2 = 0.4, f3 = 0.2, as segment 3 needs only segment 1 full
options.says: f3 = 0.2 needs w2 = 1, and w2 <= f2 then asks for f2 = 1, not 0.4.

options.text: f1 = 0, f2 = 0, f3 = 1, as the last segment may be the cheapest
options.says: f3 = 1 needs w2 = 1, which needs f2 = 1, which needs w1 = 1 and f1 = 1; the order rows forbid skipping.

origin.section: The Incremental Form Fills Segments in Order, With a Binary for Each Full One

questions.stem: In the logarithmic form, eight segments get 3-bit codes. Why must segments next to each other get codes that differ in exactly one bit?

options.text: To keep the count at three binaries for all eight segments
options.says: A plain binary count also uses three bits for eight segments; the count does not depend on the order of the codes.

options.text: To give the relaxation the same bound as the lambda form
options.says: The order of the codes is about which breakpoints each code opens; with a plain count the model allows wrong points, whatever the bound.

options.text: So the breakpoint shared by the two stays usable from both
options.says: Right: the shared breakpoint is left free by the one bit the two codes differ in, and limited the same way as both by the others.

options.text: So the solver branches on the bits in the order of segments
options.says: The codes decide which breakpoints each bit limits, not the order in which a solver branches.

origin.section: A Gray Code Picks a Segment With About log2 K Binaries

questions.stem: On one model, formulation X of a curve has 48 binaries and formulation Y has 12. Both reach the same optimum and the same LP bound. What can a planner conclude before running them?

options.text: Nothing about nodes, since binaries and bounds don't fix the count, so run both
options.says: Right: on GridCap medium the log form had the fewest binaries, and the incremental form, with almost four times as many, needed the fewest nodes.

options.text: Y needs fewer nodes, since it has a quarter of X's binaries, so run Y alone
options.says: At 16 tiers the log form's 12 binaries took 742 nodes, and the incremental form's 45 took 0.

options.text: X has a tighter LP bound, since more binaries cut more, so run X alone
options.says: The stem gives them the same LP bound, and on GridCap all three forms shared one bound whatever their binaries.

options.text: Both need the same nodes, since their LP bounds agree, so run either one
options.says: All three forms shared one LP bound on GridCap medium, and their node counts still differed by thousands.

origin.section: Fewer Binaries Is Not Fewer Nodes
